theoretical_foundations.name: Theoretical Foundations

cap_theorem.name: CAP Theorem
cap_theorem.description: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance trade-offs

consistency.description: All nodes see the same data at the same time. Every read receives the most recent write or an error.

availability.description: The system remains operational 100% of the time. Every request receives a response.

partition_tolerance.description: The system continues to operate despite network failures between nodes.

cp_systems.description: Prioritize data consistency over availability during network partitions

ap_systems.description: Prioritize system availability over immediate consistency during partitions

ca_systems.description: Traditional systems that sacrifice partition tolerance

consistency_models.name: Consistency Models
consistency_models.description: Strong, eventual, and weak consistency patterns

strong_consistency.description: All nodes see the same data at the same time. After a write operation, all subsequent reads will return the updated value.

eventual_consistency.description: The system will become consistent over time, given that the system doesn't receive new updates. Reads may return stale data temporarily.

weak_consistency.description: After a write, reads may or may not see the updated value. The system makes no guarantees about when data will be consistent.

network_partitions.description: Network failures that split the system into isolated groups, forcing trade-offs between consistency and availability.

clock_sync.description: Different nodes have different clocks, making it difficult to order events and maintain consistency.

partial_failures.description: Some parts of the system fail while others continue working, creating inconsistent states.

consensus.description: Getting distributed nodes to agree on a single value or decision in the presence of failures.

state_management.description: Keeping track of system state across multiple nodes while handling concurrent updates.

race_conditions.description: Multiple processes accessing shared resources simultaneously, leading to unpredictable results.

network_partitions.name: Network Partitions & Failures
network_partitions.description: Handling network splits and node failures

what_is.description: A network partition occurs when the network between nodes fails, splitting the system into isolated groups that cannot communicate with each other.

causes.description: Network partitions can arise from various infrastructure and configuration issues that affect connectivity between distributed nodes.

failure_types.description: Different failure modes require different detection and handling strategies in distributed systems.

fail_stop.description: Node stops completely and other nodes can detect the failure

fail_slow.description: Node becomes very slow but doesn't crash completely

datacenter_split.description: When datacenters lose connectivity, each must decide how to handle ongoing operations

service_mesh_partition.description: When services in a mesh lose connectivity to subsets of other services

database_partition.description: When database nodes become isolated from each other

detection.description: Early and accurate detection of network partitions is crucial for implementing appropriate response strategies.

prevention.description: While partitions cannot be completely prevented, their likelihood and impact can be significantly reduced through proper infrastructure design.

recovery.description: When partitions heal, systems must carefully reconcile state and resolve any conflicts that occurred during the partition.

descriptions.client: Generates the offered load (requests/s) that drives the whole system. Connect its output to your first tier (API gateway, load balancer or server). Tune "Base rate" to set how many requests per second enter the system.
descriptions.loadBalancer: Spreads incoming requests across the downstream replicas it points to, using the selected strategy (round-robin, least-connections, weighted or consistent hashing). Place it between the client/gateway and a pool of servers.
descriptions.apiGateway: Single entry point at the edge of your system. Enforces a requests/s rate limit — traffic above the limit is dropped — and forwards the rest to backends. Connect the client to it, and it to your services.
descriptions.cache: Serves a fraction of reads from memory set by "Hit rate". Hits return quickly; misses fall through to the downstream store. Put it in front of a database or service to cut load and latency.
descriptions.server: Stateless compute tier that processes requests with a given service time and concurrency. Scale it with replicas or front it with an auto-scaler. Connect it to databases, caches or other services it depends on.
descriptions.database: Persistent datastore and an end point (no outgoing edges). Its service time and concurrency make it a common bottleneck. Send read/write traffic from servers into it.
descriptions.replicatedDb: Database with multiple replicas. Writes (set by "Write fraction") hit the primary; reads spread across replicas. Pick a consistency level (strong/quorum/eventual) and replication lag to model trade-offs.
descriptions.shardRouter: Partitions traffic across shards by key using hash or range strategy. "Hot-shard skew" models one shard receiving disproportionate load. Connect it to a pool of shard backends.
descriptions.messageQueue: Buffers incoming requests and drains them at a fixed rate to smooth spikes. Messages beyond the queue capacity are dropped. Place it between a fast producer and a slower consumer.
descriptions.circuitBreaker: Wraps a downstream dependency. When the error rate exceeds the threshold it opens and sheds load for the reset timeout, then half-opens to probe recovery. Use it to stop cascading failures.
descriptions.autoScaler: Adjusts the replica count of the tier it fronts to keep utilization near the target, bounded by min/max replicas. Use it to react automatically to changing load.
descriptions.externalDependency: A third-party service you do not control (an end point). Model its latency and failure rate to simulate outages or slowdowns of upstream providers.

hints.label: Display name for this node on the canvas. Does not affect the simulation.
hints.base_rate: Requests per second this client generates. Higher = more load on the whole system; lower = lighter traffic.
hints.cron: Turn this service into a scheduled (cron) source: it generates its own work on a timer and needs no incoming connection. Use it for cron jobs, recurring workers and periodic producers.
hints.cron_rate: Self-generated requests per second when cron is on. Higher = more scheduled work injected; lower = a lighter periodic trickle.
hints.auto_scalable: Let this service scale its own replicas at runtime to hold the target utilization, bounded by min/max replicas — no separate auto-scaler node needed.
hints.service_time: Milliseconds to process one request (sets the service rate µ). Higher = slower per request, lower capacity and higher latency; lower = faster and more throughput.
hints.concurrency: Parallel workers per replica (the c in M/M/c). Higher = more requests served at once, less queueing and lower latency; lower = saturates sooner.
hints.replicas: Number of identical copies of this node (horizontal scaling). Higher = proportionally more capacity; lower = less capacity.
hints.failure_rate: Baseline probability a request fails here regardless of load. Higher = more errors propagated downstream; lower = more reliable.
hints.timeout: Milliseconds before a slow request is counted as failed. Lower = more timeouts when the node is busy; higher = waits longer before giving up.
hints.max_retries: How many times a failed call is retried. Higher = fewer final errors but more amplified load (retry storms); lower = less load but more user-visible failures.
hints.distribution: Shape of the per-request latency distribution. Lognormal has a realistic heavy tail, exponential is memoryless, deterministic is constant.
hints.variability: Coefficient of variation of latency (lognormal only). Higher = heavier tail, so p95/p99 grow; lower = more uniform latencies.
hints.strategy: How incoming requests are spread across downstream replicas (round-robin, least-connections, weighted, or consistent hashing).
hints.rate_limit: Maximum requests per second admitted; anything above is dropped. Higher = fewer drops but more load downstream; lower = protects backends but rejects traffic.
hints.hit_rate: Fraction of reads served from cache. Higher = much less load and latency downstream; lower = more requests fall through to the store.
hints.ttl: How long cached entries stay valid. Higher = more hits but staler data; lower = fresher data but more misses.
hints.queue_capacity: Maximum messages buffered. Higher = absorbs bigger spikes without dropping, but adds backlog latency; lower = drops sooner under overload.
hints.drain_rate: Messages consumed per second. Higher = backlog clears faster and latency drops; lower = backlog builds up.
hints.write_fraction: Share of operations that are writes. Higher = more load on the single primary (writes serialize), lowering effective capacity; lower = reads dominate and scale across replicas.
hints.replication_lag: Milliseconds replicas trail the primary. Higher = more stale reads with eventual consistency; lower = fresher replicas.
hints.consistency: Read/write guarantee. Strong is safest but slowest, quorum balances, eventual is fastest but can read stale data.
hints.shard_count: Number of partitions traffic is split across. Higher = more parallel capacity; lower = each shard carries more load.
hints.skew: How unevenly load lands on the hottest shard. Higher = one shard saturates and caps effective capacity; lower = balanced load.
hints.shard_strategy: How keys map to shards. Hash spreads evenly; range keeps neighbouring keys together (more prone to hotspots).
hints.error_threshold: Downstream error rate that trips the breaker open. Lower = opens sooner to protect the dependency; higher = tolerates more errors first.
hints.reset_timeout: Milliseconds the breaker stays open before probing recovery. Higher = waits longer before retrying; lower = retries the dependency sooner.
hints.target_utilization: Utilization the auto-scaler tries to hold. Lower = scales out earlier (more replicas, more headroom); higher = runs hotter with fewer replicas.
hints.min_replicas: Lower bound on replicas the auto-scaler will keep, even when idle.
hints.max_replicas: Upper bound on replicas the auto-scaler can add under load.

cache.title: Cache-Aside Simulator
cache.subtitle: Reads check the cache first. Hits return from memory; misses fall through to the database and get stored for next time.

narration.idle: Pick a key and send a read, or turn on auto traffic. Hits come from memory; misses hit the database.
narration.hit: HIT: {{key}} served from memory in {{ms}} ms. The database was never touched.
narration.miss: MISS: {{key}} is not cached. Querying the database ({{ms}} ms), then storing the result.
narration.stale: STALE: {{key}} outlived its TTL, so it counts as a miss and gets refetched.
narration.evict: Cache full: evicting least-recently-used {{key}} to make room for {{incoming}}.
narration.disabled: Cache is off: every read goes straight to the database at {{ms}} ms.

cache.hint: A cache trades freshness for speed. A high hit ratio keeps most reads in memory and shields the database; TTL and capacity decide how often you pay the slow path.

consistent_hashing.title: Consistent Hashing Simulator
consistent_hashing.subtitle: Keys on a ring — add/remove nodes and watch them remap

labels.hint: Add or remove a node — only the highlighted keys move. More virtual nodes means smoother distribution.

sharding.title: Sharding Simulator
sharding.subtitle: Route keys to shards by range or hash — and watch skew

labels.hint: Crank up skew with range partitioning to create a hot shard — then switch to hash to even it out.

inverted_index.title: Inverted Index Simulator
inverted_index.subtitle: Pick query terms and watch documents rank by score

labels.hint: AND intersects postings lists; OR unions them. Score counts how many query terms each document contains.

storage_engine.title: Storage Engine Simulator
storage_engine.subtitle: Stream writes through an LSM-tree or a B-tree and compare amplification

narration.idle: Write keys one at a time and watch where they land. LSM appends sequentially then compacts; B-tree updates pages in place.
narration.lsm_append: Write appended to the in-memory memtable ({{mem}}/{{cap}}). Sequential, so writes are cheap.
narration.lsm_flush: Memtable is full: flushed to a new immutable L0 SSTable in one sequential write.
narration.lsm_compact: {{count}} L0 SSTables merged into one L1 table ({{size}} entries rewritten). This rewrite is write amplification.
narration.btree_update: Found the leaf page for this key and rewrote page {{page}} in place. Random I/O, but reads stay a single tree walk.

btree.note: Each write seeks to a leaf page and rewrites it — random I/O.

storage_engine.hint_lsm: LSM-trees absorb writes sequentially into a memtable, then flush and compact SSTables — cheap writes, but reads may scan many tables until compaction.
storage_engine.hint_btree: B-trees update pages in place: reads are a single tree walk (low read amplification) but writes cause random I/O.

bloom_filter.title: Bloom Filter Simulator
bloom_filter.subtitle: A bit array + k hashes: fast membership tests with no false negatives

narration.idle: Insert a few keys, then query one. Each key hashes to k bit positions; watch which bits get set and how queries are answered.
narration.inserted: Inserted "{{word}}": its k hashes point to bits {{positions}}, now set to 1.
narration.maybe: "{{word}}": all {{k}} hashed bits are 1, so it is probably present (could still be a collision).
narration.false_positive: "{{word}}" was never inserted, yet all its bits are 1 because other keys set them. That is a false positive.
narration.absent: "{{word}}": bit {{pos}} is 0, so it is definitely not present. Bloom filters never give false negatives.

result.maybe: is probably present (all k bits set).
result.false_positive: reads as present, but was never inserted. False positive!
result.definitely_not: is definitely not present (at least one bit is 0).

bloom_filter.hint: A query is "maybe present" only if every hashed bit is 1. More items or fewer bits raise the false-positive rate; there are never false negatives.

quorum_replication.title: Quorum Replication Simulator
quorum_replication.subtitle: Tune replicas (N), write quorum (W), and read quorum (R)

narration.idle: Write a new version to W nodes, then read from R nodes, and watch whether the read quorum overlaps the latest write.
narration.wrote: Wrote v{{version}} to a write quorum of W={{w}} nodes. The other replicas still hold older versions.
narration.read_fresh: The read quorum R={{r}} overlapped the write quorum at {{count}} node(s), so it returned the freshest v{{value}}. R+W>N forces that overlap.
narration.read_stale: The read quorum R={{r}} missed every node holding the latest write, so it returned a stale v{{value}}. With R+W not greater than N the quorums can miss each other.

quorum_replication.hint: When R + W > N the read and write quorums always overlap, so reads see the newest write. Lower them for higher availability at the cost of stale reads.

cdc.title: CDC Simulator
cdc.subtitle: A connector tails the database log and ships changes to downstream sinks

narration.idle: Start the stream. The connector tails the DB log in order and ships each change to every downstream sink.
narration.shipping: Connector shipped {{k}} change(s) downstream. Replication lag is {{lag}}.
narration.lagging: Writes ({{rate}}/tick) outpace the connector ({{crate}}/tick), so the log grows behind the offset. Lag is now {{lag}}.
narration.caught_up: The connector is keeping up: lag is {{lag}} and the sinks are in sync with the source.

cdc.wal_note: Amber = behind the offset (not yet captured); green = already shipped downstream
cdc.hint: If writes outpace the connector, lag grows and downstream sinks fall behind. CDC keeps caches, search, and analytics in sync without dual writes.

kafka.title: Kafka Simulator
kafka.subtitle: Producers, partitions, and a consumer group — watch the lag

labels.hint: Each partition is read by exactly one consumer. Add consumers beyond the partition count and they sit idle — partitions cap parallelism.

api_styles.title: API Styles Simulator
api_styles.subtitle: Fetch a screen of data with REST, GraphQL, or gRPC and compare the cost

narration.rest: REST returned all 12 user fields across {{rt}} round trip(s); the screen used {{used}}, so {{over}}% was over-fetched.
narration.graphql: GraphQL returned exactly the {{used}} field(s) the screen asked for in one round trip, no over-fetching.
narration.grpc: gRPC returned {{used}} field(s) as compact binary in one round trip, roughly a third the size of JSON.

hint.rest: REST often needs one request per resource and returns whole objects — simple and cacheable, but it over-fetches and may need several round trips.
hint.graphql: GraphQL gets exactly the requested fields in a single round trip — no over-fetching, at the cost of server-side query planning.
hint.grpc: gRPC sends compact binary Protobuf over one round trip with a strict schema — fastest on the wire, but not human-readable and harder to debug.

realtime_push.title: Real-Time Push Simulator
realtime_push.subtitle: Deliver server events with polling, SSE, or WebSockets

narration.idle: Pick a transport and run it. Watch how server events reach the client, and what each approach costs.
narration.poll_deliver: A poll arrived and collected {{k}} queued event(s). They had waited up to {{interval}} ticks for this request.
narration.poll_empty: A poll arrived but the server had nothing new, a wasted empty request.
narration.push: The server pushed the event the instant it happened over the open connection, about 1 tick of latency.

hint.polling: Polling re-asks on a fixed interval: simple, but adds latency (up to one interval) and wastes requests when nothing changed.
hint.sse: Server-Sent Events push one-way over a single long-lived HTTP connection — near-instant delivery with almost no request overhead.
hint.websocket: WebSockets keep a full-duplex connection open — instant, bidirectional delivery ideal for chat, games, and live collaboration.

dead_letter_queue.title: Dead Letter Queue Simulator
dead_letter_queue.subtitle: Failed messages retry, then move to the DLQ after the limit

narration.idle: Run the queue. Failed messages are retried; once they pass the retry limit they move to the DLQ so they cannot block the queue forever.
narration.retry: Message #{{id}} failed (attempt {{n}}/{{max}}), re-queued for another try.
narration.dlq: Message #{{id}} hit the retry limit after {{n}} attempts, moved to the DLQ. The queue keeps flowing.

dead_letter_queue.hint: Transient failures are retried; once a message exceeds the retry limit (or is a poison message) it goes to the DLQ instead of blocking the queue forever.

saga.title: Saga Simulator
saga.subtitle: A distributed transaction as a sequence of compensable steps

labels.hint: A saga has no global rollback. When a step fails, each completed step is undone by its own compensating action, in reverse order.
At-most-once can lose messages; at-least-once can duplicate them. "Exactly-once" = at-least-once delivery plus deduplication on the consumer.

crdt.title: CRDT Simulator (G-Counter)
crdt.subtitle: Increment replicas independently, then merge — they always converge

narration.idle: Increment any replica. Each counts only in its own slot, so the replicas drift apart until they gossip.
narration.increment: Replica {{replica}} counted +1 in its own slot and now reads {{total}}. The others have not heard yet, so values diverge.
narration.merge: {{a}} and {{b}} gossiped: each slot becomes the max of the two. No increment is ever lost, and merge order never changes the result.
narration.converged: Every replica now holds the same vector and agrees on {{total}}. Eventually consistent, with zero conflict resolution.

crdt.all_agree: All replicas agree on the value.
crdt.need_sync: Replicas hold different values, gossip to merge.
crdt.hint: Each replica counts its own increments in its own slot. Merge takes the element-wise max, so increments are never lost and any merge order yields the same result.

gossip.title: Gossip Simulator
gossip.subtitle: One node learns an update; it spreads epidemically across the cluster

narration.idle: One node knows the update. Press Start to let it gossip, or Step through one round at a time.
narration.round: Round {{round}}: {{senders}} informed node(s) gossiped to {{peers}} peer(s). Now {{known}}/{{total}} know.
narration.converged: Converged in {{rounds}} rounds. Coverage roughly doubles each round, so the cluster syncs in about log₂(N) rounds.

gossip.hint: Each informed node tells a few random peers each round, so the update reaches everyone in about log(N) rounds, with no coordinator, and it tolerates failures.

distributed_lock.title: Distributed Lock Simulator
distributed_lock.subtitle: A lease-based lock with fencing tokens that reject stale writers

narration.idle: Acquire the lock, stall the holder until its lease expires, let another client acquire, then write from the stalled client to watch fencing reject the stale token. Or run the demo.
narration.acquire: Client {{client}} acquired the lock with fencing token {{token}} (a monotonically increasing number).
narration.stall: Client {{client}} stalled (e.g. a GC pause). Its lease keeps ticking and will expire while it is frozen.
narration.expired: The lease expired and the lock auto-released.
narration.expired_stalled: The lease expired and the lock auto-released, but the stalled holder still thinks it owns the lock.
narration.write_ok: Client {{client}} wrote with token {{token}} (>= resource token {{rt}}): accepted. The resource advances to {{token}}.
narration.fenced: Client {{client}} wrote with stale token {{token}} (< resource token {{rt}}): fenced. The resource rejects the old token.

distributed_lock.hint: Acquire the lock, stall the holder until its lease expires, let another client acquire (higher token), then write from the stalled client — the resource fences the stale, lower token.

philosophers_sim.title: Dining Philosophers
philosophers_sim.subtitle: Five philosophers share five forks. Eating needs both neighbouring forks, so the seats compete for the same resource. Pick a strategy and watch how it avoids — or causes — deadlock.

naive.label: Naive
naive.desc: Each philosopher grabs the left fork, then waits for the right one. If everyone picks up their left fork at once, all hold one fork forever — a textbook deadlock.

hierarchy.label: Resource Hierarchy
hierarchy.desc: Forks are numbered; a philosopher always acquires the lower-numbered fork first. Breaking the circular-wait condition makes deadlock impossible.

atomic.label: Both or Nothing
atomic.desc: A philosopher only picks up forks when both are free, atomically. Nobody ever holds a single fork, so there is no deadlock (starvation is still possible).

arbitrator.label: Central Arbitrator
arbitrator.desc: A waiter lets at most N-1 philosophers reach for forks at the same time. With one seat always free, the circular wait can never close.

viz.title: The Table
viz.deadlock_hint: Deadlock detected: every hungry philosopher holds one fork and waits forever for the other. Reset and try a deadlock-free strategy.

log.title: Event Log
log.started_eating: {{name}} grabbed both forks and started eating
log.finished_eating: {{name}} finished eating and released the forks
log.deadlock_detected: Deadlock detected — no philosopher can make progress

algo_desc.token: Tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one. Allows bursts up to the bucket size.
algo_desc.leaky: Requests fill a fixed queue that drains at a constant rate. Smooths output; rejects when the queue is full.
algo_desc.sliding: Counts requests in the trailing 1s window; rejects once the limit is reached. No bursts beyond the limit.

info.title: Explanation
info.p1: This simulator demonstrates how retry mechanisms work in distributed systems. Each attempt has a success chance based on the configured rate.
info.p2: With exponential backoff, the time between attempts increases progressively (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...), reducing system load.
info.p3: Jitter adds a random variation to the time between attempts, preventing multiple clients from retrying at the exact same time.

strategies.least_conn: Least Connections: Sends new requests to the server with the lowest current load.

outbox.title: Transactional Outbox Simulator
outbox.subtitle: Dual-write vs the outbox pattern when the broker is flaky

narration.idle: Place an order and follow it through. Raise the broker failure rate to see how each approach copes.
narration.dual_ok: Order #{{n}}: committed to the DB, then the event published to the broker. Both succeeded this time.
narration.dual_lost: Order #{{n}}: committed to the DB, but the broker was down so the publish failed. That event is lost forever, the DB and broker now disagree.
narration.outbox_commit: Order #{{n}}: the order and its outbox row committed in one transaction. The relay will publish it next.
narration.outbox_drain: Order #{{n}} committed atomically; the relay published {{k}} queued outbox row(s) to the broker.
narration.outbox_wait: Order #{{n}}: committed atomically. The broker is down, so the outbox row waits safely in the DB, nothing is lost.

hint.dual-write: With a dual write, the DB commit and the publish are separate. When the broker fails after the commit, the event is lost forever — the DB and broker diverge.
hint.outbox: The outbox writes the event into the same transaction as the data. A relay publishes it with retries, so nothing is lost — only delayed when the broker is down.

bulkhead.title: Bulkhead Simulator
bulkhead.subtitle: One slow dependency should not sink unrelated traffic

narration.shared: One shared pool of {{pool}} workers serves both dependencies. Right now {{used}} slots are in use.
narration.starved: Slow B calls are holding {{busyB}} of the shared slots, so healthy A calls now get rejected. One slow dependency sinks everything.
narration.bulkhead: A and B each own half the pool. B’s slowness fills only its own slots, so A keeps serving normally.

bulkhead.shared_note: Shared pool: slow B calls hold every worker, so healthy A calls get rejected too.
bulkhead.bulkhead_note: Bulkheads: A and B each get half the pool, so B’s slowness is contained and A keeps serving.
bulkhead.hint: Without isolation, a slow dependency exhausts the shared pool and takes down healthy traffic. Bulkheads cap each dependency so failures stay contained.

pacelc.title: PACELC Simulator
pacelc.subtitle: If Partition: choose A or C. Else (normal ops): choose L or C.

outcomes.PA: During a partition, the system stays available and serves possibly-stale data on both sides (e.g. Dynamo, Cassandra).
outcomes.PC: During a partition, the system refuses requests on the minority side to preserve consistency (e.g. MongoDB, HBase).
outcomes.EL: In normal operation, the system answers from the nearest replica for low latency, accepting weaker consistency (e.g. Dynamo).
outcomes.EC: In normal operation, the system coordinates replicas for strong consistency, paying extra latency (e.g. MongoDB, Bigtable).

pacelc.hint: PACELC extends CAP: a partition forces A-vs-C, but Else (the common case, no partition) you still trade Latency vs Consistency. Many systems pick the same side in both — PA/EL or PC/EC.

chaos.title: Chaos Engineering Simulator
chaos.subtitle: Inject failures into a cluster and measure whether resilience holds

narration.idle: All nodes are healthy. Kill a node or run a game day to test whether the system survives failure.
narration.resilient: {{down}} node(s) down, but replicas and retries reroute around them, so availability holds at {{avail}}%.
narration.degraded: {{down}} node(s) down and requests are pinned to nodes, so availability has dropped to {{avail}}%.

chaos.hint_on: With replicas and retries, requests reroute to healthy nodes — killing a node barely dents availability. This is the goal: failures are non-events.
chaos.hint_off: Without redundancy, requests pinned to a dead node fail outright. Every node you kill drops availability proportionally — exactly the weakness chaos testing exposes.

algorithms.title: Synchronization Algorithms
algorithms.intro: There are several algorithms to ensure synchronization in distributed systems. Each has specific characteristics and ideal use cases.
algorithms.key_concept_text: The choice of synchronization algorithm depends on factors such as number of nodes, network latency, fault tolerance, and performance requirements.

bakery.title: Bakery Algorithm
bakery.concept_p: Based on a bakery where each customer receives a ticket number and is served in increasing order.

token_ring.title: Token Ring
token_ring.concept_p: A token circulates among processes in a logical ring, and only the process holding the token can access shared resources.

ricart_agrawala.title: Ricart-Agrawala
ricart_agrawala.concept_p: Based on logical timestamps, where processes request permission from all others before accessing shared resources.

logs.title: Logs and Tracing in Distributed Systems
logs.intro_p1: Logs and tracing are essential to understand behavior, debug issues, and maintain observability. They provide detailed insights into execution flow and system state.
logs.key_concept_text: In distributed systems, logs should be treated as event streams, centralized and correlated to provide a complete system view.
logs.structured_desc: Structured logging treats logs as data objects rather than plain text, enabling easier analysis and search.

logs_page.title: Logs and Tracing in Distributed Systems
logs_page.intro_p1: In distributed systems, logs and tracing are fundamental for monitoring, debugging, and performance analysis. This section explores best practices and tools to implement a robust observability system.

tracing_section.title: Distributed Tracing
tracing_section.what_is_p: Tracing tracks the path of a request across multiple services in a distributed system. Each request receives a unique ID (traceId) that is propagated across services.

attack_simulator.title: Attack Simulator
attack_simulator.subtitle: Explore interactively how different types of attacks work in distributed systems. This simulator visually demonstrates the behavior and impact of DDoS and Man-in-the-Middle attacks.
how_to_use_steps: Select the type of attack you want to simulate (DDoS or Man-in-the-Middle)
Adjust the simulation speed as needed
Click "Start Simulation" to begin the visualization
Observe the packet behavior and impact on the server
simulator_elements: Legitimate clients trying to access the service
attack_simulator.ddos_simulation_description: This simulation shows how multiple attackers overwhelm a server with malicious traffic, making it difficult for legitimate users to access the service. The server becomes overloaded when receiving many requests.
attack_simulator.mitm_simulation_description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can intercept communication between client and server by positioning themselves in the middle of the connection. The attacker can read and modify transmitted data.
